display.text: A pattern in which values of one variable are related to values of another; it does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
A relationship in which changing one variable produces a change in another, rather than merely accompanying it. Also called causal relationship.
A situation in which the effects of an explanatory variable and another variable on the response cannot be distinguished adequately.
A comparison group handled similarly to a treatment group but without the active treatment of interest, sometimes receiving a placebo.
Accounting for another variable when examining a relationship, such as by comparing groups separately at similar values of that variable.
The extent to which a study's setting and findings reflect the situations in which the behavior ordinarily occurs.
A study in which researchers impose treatments or values of an explanatory variable and observe the response.
Influence of researchers' expectations or knowledge of treatment assignments on how responses are assessed or recorded.
An explanatory variable in an experiment whose values are set by the researchers.
A variable outside the analysis that could substantially change the interpretation of the relationship between the explanatory and response variables.
Failure of participants to follow the treatment or condition assigned to them, potentially undermining the intended experimental comparison.
A study that records variables as they occur naturally without assigning the explanatory variable's values.
An inactive treatment made to resemble an active treatment, providing a comparison for effects associated with receiving treatment and expecting improvement.
A change in response associated with the belief or expectation of receiving treatment rather than with the active treatment component.
An observational study that records exposures or explanatory values and follows outcomes forward in time.
Using chance to select people from a population, supporting generalization rather than itself establishing a treatment's causal effect.
An experiment in which researchers use random assignment to compare imposed treatments, supporting causal interpretation when the design is implemented well.
An observational study that looks backward at past measurements, records, or recollections to examine relationships.
A study that obtains information by asking a sample of individuals questions, including self-reports or self-assessments.
A reversal in the direction of an association when data are separated into groups defined by another variable rather than combined.
A condition or value of an experimental factor imposed on participants to evaluate its effect on the response. Abbreviated ttt.
The participants assigned to receive a particular experimental treatment or condition.
